subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition D (Changes to Ballot Measure Process)

strong: Shall the City amend the Charter to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters in San Francisco (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for calling special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn before an election, and remove the ability of a minority of Board of Supervisors members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot?

text: This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
How “D” Got on the Ballot

On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition D to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

The San Francisco Board of Supervisors (Board) has 11 members. A measure can be either an ordinance to change the law or a declaration of policy. Under the City Charter, measures can be placed on the ballot in several ways, including:
By a majority vote of the Board;
By four or more Board members without a Board vote;
By the Mayor without a Board vote; or
By a signature initiative (petition) signed by at least 2% of the registered voters in San Francisco, currently about 10,600 signatures.
Currently San Francisco has over 530,000 registered voters.
Signature initiatives usually appear on the ballot at the next regularly scheduled election.

Signature initiatives may call for an earlier “special” election on an ordinance if the petition is signed by at least 10% of the votes cast for all candidates for Mayor in the last election. Currently, this is about 39,000 signatures.
Once a signature initiative is submitted to the Department of Elections, it cannot be withdrawn.
Proposition D would amend the Charter to increase the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:

Increasing the number of signatures required to place a signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco.

Increasing the number of signatures required to call a special election on an ordinance from 10% of the votes cast for Mayor in the last election to 10% of the registered voters in San Francisco. Currently, this is about 53,100 signatures.
Proposition D would allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn up to 102 days before the election.
Proposition D would also change the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
Removing the ability of four or more Board members to place a measure on the ballot without a Board vote;
Removing the ability of the Mayor to independently place a measure on the ballot;
The Board could still place measures on the ballot by a majority vote.

If you vote “yes,” you want to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn, and remove the ability of a minority of Board members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot.
If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition D:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government.

The proposed Charter amendment would (1) require the approval of a majority of the Board of Supervisors to place an ordinance on the ballot, (2) eliminate the Mayor’s ability to directly place an ordinance on the ballot, (3) increase the voter signature threshold for initiatives from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco, (4) allow proponents to withdraw a measure after it qualifies for the ballot, and (5) raise the threshold for special elections from 10% of the votes for mayor in the last general municipal election to 10% of registered voters.

The proposed amendment is likely to reduce costs at levels that cannot be determined at this time. Since the proposed Charter amendment raises the voter signature threshold, fewer initiatives may qualify for the ballot which may reduce the volume of printed pages included in the voter information pamphlet (VIP). On average, each page in the VIP costs $11,400 to prepare, print, and distribute to all registered voters. The proposed increase in the voter signature threshold may also reduce the number of special elections called which would result in cost savings for the Department of Elections. The estimated minimum cost for a citywide special election is $5 million with a one-card ballot and less than 50-page VIP.

The proposed Charter amendment may impact the Department of Elections’ workload. It may result in a reduction in ballot ordinances which would reduce the associated workload for the Department of Elections—freeing staff to work on other government functions. Conversely, the Department of Elections may see an increase in workload to validate more voter signatures for a measure to qualify for the ballot and to remove qualified measures at the proponents’ request.
Clean Up City Hall is a package of Props A, D, E and F to improve neighborhood services, speed up permitting and reduce wasteful spending so we can invest in our great city.

arguments.title: NO ON D: DON’T ROB OUR RIGHT TO VOTE.

text: This isn’t about streamlining or state standards. Prop D takes away rights San Franciscans have held for 125 years: to put citizen initiatives on the ballot.

San Francisco was the first California city to have this right. Now, wealthy tech billionaires are spending millions to take it away. They would quadruple the signatures required from 10,600 to 42,500, a limit so high only the very wealthy can reach it.

Wealthy interests can afford to pay one million dollars to collect 42,500 signatures. Neighborhood groups, labor unions and community advocates will be priced out. We’ll lose our voice in the democratic process.

Since 1932, around 10,600 signatures have been required to qualify a measure. It’s not easy: citizen-initiatives are only 15% of all ballot measures. But when City Hall ignores us, citizens have the power to act. A check and balance.
It will be impossible for citizen-led, grassroots organizations to qualify a measure. After 125 years, it will silence the voices of some San Franciscans forever.

They have increased the minimum wage, ensured large corporations pay their fair share of taxes, provided legal aid for renters facing eviction, banned corrupt contributions to politicians, passed Sunshine laws, established rent control, and funded schools, childcare and affordable housing.
After 125 years of direct democracy, don’t let them rob it away. Vote NO on D.

arguments.title: D ENDS THE INSIDER MONOPOLY ON POWER AT THE BALLOT

text: The insiders are misleading voters because their monopoly on power is being challenged. They think the system works great. San Franciscans know the system is broken: keeping us in a constant state of confusion, dividing neighbors, and producing bad outcomes.

D is a set of modest reforms requiring transparency, compromise, and community input before issues get on the ballot so that voters can weigh in on well thought-out measures. None of these reforms add a financial cost.

Currently a minority of supervisors, just 2% of voters, or the mayor acting alone can throw anything on the ballot without public input, transparency, or proven community support. Political insiders exploit these rules regularly. That is why San Francisco has the longest and most confusing ballots in the state.

With D, placing a measure on the ballot requires a public vote of a majority of the Supervisors or a modest amount of signatures. D also removes the mayor’s sole authority to place measures on the ballot, ensuring a fair balance of power.

Opponents claim today’s rules date to 1932. The Controller’s report confirms the current threshold was set in 2022, requiring approximately 9,000 fewer signatures than before. San Francisco will still have one of the lowest signature thresholds in California, including other large cities like Oakland, San Diego, and Long Beach.

arguments.title: Fewer Measures. Better Decisions.

text: San Francisco voters face some of the longest, most complicated ballots in California — 15 local measures in November 2024 alone, compared to 3 in Oakland and 1 in San José. Since 1996, San Franciscans have voted on 418 local measures, nearly half placed on the ballot without the ordinary legislative process of public hearings and Board approval.

This reform comes straight from SPUR’s Charter for Change (2026), building on recommendations SPUR first raised in Designed to Serve (2024) and on SPUR’s long history of advocating for smarter, more deliberate lawmaking in San Francisco, including its sponsorship of 2007’s ballot-sunshine reforms.

The measure ends the practice of the Mayor or just four Supervisors placing measures directly on the ballot without majority Board support — a power no other major California city grants. It raises the citizen signature threshold from 2% to 8% of registered voters, still lower than Oakland, San Diego, Sacramento, and most California cities. And it lets initiative sponsors withdraw measures before an election, opening the door to negotiated solutions instead of costly campaigns.

Complex policy deserves public hearings and negotiation, not an up-or-down vote squeezed between a dozen other measures. This measure lets City Hall do its job, reserving the ballot for issues that truly need a public vote.

text: GOOD GOVERNANCE LEADERS AGREE PROP D WILL IMPROVE VOTER TRUST.

A healthy democracy depends on a ballot voters can trust— one with proposals made with real community support, not political maneuvering. San Francisco’s current system falls far short. It requires 80% fewer signatures than the state standard, meaning a small minority of politicians and private interests can flood the ballot with contradictory measures designed to confuse voters and settle political scores. We’ve seen how this plays out: instead of building coalitions and answering hard questions publicly, insiders can target a handful of supervisors to get a measure on the ballot.

Prop D protects the ballot from manipulation. It requires a majority of the Board of Supervisors or signatures from 8% of voters — much closer to the state’s 10% standard — and removes the mayor’s power to unilaterally place measures on the ballot, which no other California cities had to start with. It also lets proponents withdraw measures, allowing space to reach agreements or correct for flaws or unintended consequences instead of leaving voters to clean up the mess.

This is a structural fix for a structural problem: a process that currently rewards insider access instead of genuine coalition-building and public vetting. Good government and a functioning democracy means a ballot voters can trust. Prop D gets us there.

text: LABOR LEADERS SAY YES ON D FOR BETTER RESULTS AT THE BALLOT.

Working people don’t have lobbyists on retainer — we build power through coalitions, organizing, and showing up. San Francisco’s ballot process currently rewards the opposite. It makes it easy for a small group of politicians to put divisive, intentionally confusing measures forward without building real public support. Under the current system, private interests can skip community organizing altogether and just lobby a few supervisors to put measures before voters. Those with the most access use that shortcut instead of doing the work of earning broad support, the way labor always has.

Prop D levels the playing field. A ballot process that rewards coalition-building over insider access is a ballot process that works better for working people and the organizations that represent us. Labor believes in earning support the real way. Vote Yes on Prop D for a fair, transparent democracy.

text: SMALL AND BIG BUSINESSES URGE BUILDING CONSENSUS MEASURES THROUGH PROP D.

San Francisco’s ballot has become a magnet for divisive, contradictory measures — and businesses trying to plan, invest, and operate here bear the cost of that unstable operating environment. The current rules make it far too easy to flood the ballot with measures that cancel each other out or exist mainly to settle political scores.

A more honest, transparent ballot process means fewer contradictory measures, less wasted money, and a more predictable policy environment for the businesses that call San Francisco home. San Francisco’s business community supports a ballot process built on real coalition-building, not insider access: Vote Yes on Prop D.

text: CHINATOWN LEADERS URGE YES ON D FOR A BETTER DEMOCRACY.

Chinatown and immigrant communities have long known that the loudest, best-connected voices too often win at City Hall — including on the ballot itself. San Francisco requires far fewer signatures than the state standard, making it easy for insiders to flood the ballot with measures that are intentionally written to confuse and divide in ways that voters, especially those navigating language barriers, should not have to grapple with.

An honest, vetted ballot process means fewer confusing measures and a system that rewards communities who organize and build coalitions instead of those with insider access. Chinatown deserves a ballot voters can actually trust and understand. Vote Yes on Prop D for a fairer, more transparent process.

arguments.title: 42,500 signatures is easy for wealthy interests, impossible for everyone else. Vote No on D

text: Prop D is a dangerous measure that uses positive language — “streamlining, simplifying” — to obscure its true function: raising the signature threshold for citizen initiatives from 10,600 to 42,500, nearly quadrupling the effort and expense required to qualify a measure for the ballot. Deep-pocketed special interests who can afford professional signature-gathering firms will still be able to place initiatives on the ballot — even frivolous ones — while grassroots campaigns, labor unions, and community groups are locked out entirely.
Since 1932, San Francisco has required an average of 10,000 signatures, giving citizens access to the ballot. Don’t let them take this vital safeguard away. No on D!

text: PRESERVE CITIZEN DEMOCRACY-VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION
Is our initiative process “broken” because it allows citizens to persuade 10,600 voters (2% of registered voters) to petition for a ballot proposition?
Should we “fix” this by requiring more nearly 42,500 signatures (8% of registered voters)?

This increase will, undoubtedly, result in fewer citizen led initiatives. But corporations or dark-money PACs, who hire people to harvest signatures for their propositions, won’t be stopped. Do we really want to discourage citizen groups from even trying?
Some say that our initiative process is “broken” because we allow ordinary citizens to vote on matters that may, to outsiders, seem trivial, such as closing a highway.
The alternative view is that San Francisco is so democratic that we allow ordinary citizens to override bureaucrats on such matters of direct concern to the public.

More than a hundred years ago, John Dewey famously said, “the cure for the ills of democracy is more democracy.” This proposal, however, argues that the solution is less democracy, less citizen involvement.
I encourage you to vote NO.

text: Keep Resident Control of our Government - Vote No on D

The Mayor has allied with billionaires to weaken our voices in our own government by proposing a quadrupling of resident signatures needed to place measures on the ballot. Citizen initiatives have saved our parks and neighborhoods, funded affordable housing and provided critical services to our neighbors. Reducing resident voices in our government would tip our politics into a playground for billionaires, increasing their power while reducing ours.
Vote NO on D
